claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles have a size-dependent thermal response.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit surface atomic diffusion at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Surface atomic diffusion is more pronounced in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles than in larger nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo phase separation earlier during heating than larger nanoparticles.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are a homogeneous solid solution at room temperature.
Pulsed laser deposition is a possible synthesis route for the stated initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
In situ heating electron microscopy can be used to investigate the atomic-scale thermal response of HEA nanoparticles.
Molecular dynamics simulations can complement in situ heating microscopy in studying HEA nanoparticle thermal behavior.
A temperature interval from approximately 298 to 973 K is suitable for monitoring thermally induced changes in HEA nanoparticles.
The experiment is conducted under high vacuum on a TEM heating chip with SiN membranes.
Heating FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles produces pronounced atomic diffusion at their surfaces.
Surface atomic diffusion leads to segregated surface layers or phase domains.
Increasing temperature increases atomic mobility and drives phase separation in HEA nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have a larger surface-to-volume ratio than larger nanoparticles.
The larger surface-to-volume ratio of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles accelerates atomic diffusion.
Accelerated diffusion in smaller nanoparticles causes an earlier onset of structural transformation.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit melting phenomena earlier than larger nanoparticles.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles retain structural homogeneity to higher temperatures.
At room temperature, the FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are random, nearly equiatomic solid solutions without observable phase separation.
A controlled vacuum environment prevents extraneous chemical reactions such as oxidation during heating.
